The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Spangled emperor (Lethrinus nebulosus) has been estimated at approximately 8% [GSI = approximately 8%] for reproductively active individuals sampled in waters at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The index was derived from gravid females collected during the summer spawning aggregation, when water temperatures consistently reached this thermal optimum. Such a low value is characteristic of iteroparous reef fishes that spawn repeatedly over an extended season rather than investing heavily in a single massive batch of gametes. Field observations indicate that individuals with elevated condition factors tend to exhibit slightly higher indices, though the population mean remains stable across successive years. These findings provide a useful baseline for comparing reproductive allocation strategies among sympatric lethrinid species occupying similar coral reef habitats.

Hatchlings of Lethrinus nebulosus emerge from pelagic eggs at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.00018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00018 grams], a value derived from an average egg diameter of 0.7 millimeters based on data from the closely related Lethrinus lentjan. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the typical reproductive strategy of tropical spariform fishes, which produce large numbers of small, yolk-dependent larvae that drift in the plankton before settling into benthic habitats. The newly hatched prolarvae are entirely endotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves during their first days of development. Following the onset of exogenous feeding, growth proceeds rapidly under optimal thermal conditions, with larvae attaining sizes sufficient for reef settlement within a few weeks. The egg diameter itself, approximately 0.7 mm, is consistent with the range reported for other members of the family Lethrinidae. This small initial body size imposes a high vulnerability to planktonic predators, a constraint that is offset by high fecundity and a protracted spawning season that ensures some larval cohorts encounter favorable conditions for survival and recruitment.

As individuals of Spangled emperor progress through their life cycle, they attain a total length at puberty of 38.8 centimeters [Lp = 38.8 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the onset of gonadal maturation in both sexes. This length marks the transition from the juvenile to the adult phase, after which fish begin allocating energy toward gamete production rather than exclusively toward somatic growth. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from the length-weight relationship for this species, is approximately 922 grams [Wwp = approximately 922 grams], indicating that fish must accumulate substantial body reserves before reproductive maturation becomes energetically feasible. Puberty is typically reached between two and three years of age in the wild, depending on local growth rates and food availability. Individuals inhabiting regions with lower productivity may delay maturation until they attain a larger size, while those in more resource-rich environments may mature slightly earlier. The length at puberty is significantly smaller than the ultimate total length reported for this species, suggesting a prolonged period of adult growth following reproductive onset. This pattern is common among iteroparous reef fishes that continue to increase in body size throughout much of their reproductive lifespan.

The ultimate total length recorded for Lethrinus nebulosus reaches 87 centimeters [Li = 87 centimeters], representing the maximum size individuals can achieve under natural conditions. This impressive length corresponds to an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 10,226 grams [Wwi = approximately 10,226 grams], derived from the established length-weight relationship for the species. Such a large adult body size places the Spangled emperor among the larger members of its genus, with only a few congeners surpassing it in maximum dimensions. The species exhibits indeterminate growth, meaning that individuals continue to increase in length throughout their lives, albeit at a decreasing rate as they approach this asymptotic maximum. The growth trajectory is well described by the von Bertalanffy equation, with parameters that reflect a moderately fast-growing fish that attains about half its ultimate length within the first few years of life. Large adults are typically found in deeper reef habitats and are less vulnerable to predation than smaller conspecifics. The ultimate size achieved is influenced by environmental factors such as food availability and water temperature, with individuals from more productive regions often reaching larger asymptotic lengths.

For Spangled emperor individuals maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is 28 years [am = 28 years], a longevity that is notable among tropical lethrinids. This estimate is based on annual otolith increment counts from individuals collected across the species range, with the oldest documented specimen showing 28 growth zones. A longevity of 28 years [am = 28 years], combined with iteroparous reproduction, suggests a life-history strategy that spreads reproductive effort across multiple decades, buffering against years of poor recruitment at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Older individuals tend to attain the largest body sizes and likely contribute disproportionately to overall fecundity due to their greater mass and egg production capacity. The species shows no evidence of reproductive senescence, with even the oldest females continuing to produce viable gametes. This extended longevity is consistent with the low natural mortality rates observed in unfished populations. Comparative data from otolith-based studies indicate that other lethrinid species of similar body size often exhibit lifespans ranging from 15 to 25 years, making the Spangled emperor one of the longer-lived members of its family. Such a lifespan, coupled with slow maturation, underscores the species vulnerability to overfishing.
